title: The quail and the hawk
hookLine: a quail safe in its own field is caught when it strays (SN 47.6)

lines: A QUAIL IN THE HAWK'S CLAWS.
A PLOWED FIELD, FULL OF CLODS.
cards: A hawk drops out of the sky and comes up with a quail in its claws. And the quail, being carried off, starts talking. Not begging.
Scolding itself. This is my own fault, it says. I wandered out of my own range into somebody else's.
If I'd stayed in my home ground, the ground my mother and father knew, this hawk would be no match for me. The hawk, apparently amused, asks: and where is this home ground of yours?
A plowed field, says the quail, covered with clods of earth.

teach.h: THE HAWK LETS THE QUAIL GO.
teach.b: This is SN 47.6, in the Connected Discourses on mindfulness. The hawk, proud of its strength, lets the quail go. Fine, it says.
Go home. Even there you won't escape me.

teach.h: A CLOD IN A PLOWED FIELD.
teach.b: The quail flies back to its plowed field, climbs onto a big clod of earth, and calls up: come and get me now, hawk. The hawk folds its wings and dives at full speed.
The quail watches it come, and at the last moment slips down behind the clod. The hawk hits the earth breast first. Then the Buddha explains.
Don't wander outside your own range, monks, into the range of others. In others' ground, Mara, the tempter, gets his chance.
Others' range is the five cords of sense pleasure: sights, sounds, smells, tastes and touches that pull at desire.
Your own range, the ground your fathers knew, is the four foundations of mindfulness: the body, feelings, the mind, and the patterns of experience. The quail isn't stronger than the hawk.
It simply knows its ground, every furrow, every clod. Safety in this story isn't power; it's familiarity.

teach.h: GOCARA — A PASTURE KNOWN BY HEART.
teach.b: And the text's word for range is gocara, a pasture, the ground a grazing animal knows by heart.
Mindfulness isn't a fortress you build. It's a field you know so well you can disappear into it. The hawk doesn't stop being a hawk.
What changes is where the quail is standing when one comes.

how: In many Buddhist communities, mindfulness is described as a practitioner's own ground or home base, returned to through the day; monastics often keep simple routines and guard the senses when they go into town as a way of staying in that range.

o: your own range, ground you know by heart
a hawk's hunting ground in open country
a hidden shelter for monks in the forest

games.q: who did what, and what it stands for.
p: slips behind a clod in its field
the five cords of sense pleasure

s: the quail wins because it is stronger than the hawk
it wins because it knows its ground and slips behind a clod.
in this sutta, your own range means the four foundations of mindfulness
body, feelings, mind and the patterns of experience: the ground your fathers knew.
the hawk gives up hunting at the end
the story never says so; the quail just stands where the hawk can't reach it.

games.q: you're a quail, caught by a hawk. the hawk lets you go home, sure it can catch you anyway. what do you do?
o: fly as far away as you can
go to your plowed field, stand on a clod, and wait
beg the hawk to leave you alone
games.why: the quail stands on a clod in its own field and calls the hawk down. at the last moment it slips behind the clod, and the hawk hits the earth.

practice: Make your field small, the breath and the body sitting, and get to know its clods: where the breath touches first, where the body is heavy.
When a thought flies off toward someone else's field, a plan, a worry, a screen, notice that you've left, and come back to one clod you know: one breath, one point of contact.

wordCard.voice: Gocara, range or pasture. Safety isn't strength; it's staying in your own range, the four foundations of mindfulness.

orig.note: Pali gocara: range, pasture, the ground a grazing animal knows; the sutta's word for your own range.

carryVoice: Your line: your own ground. The quail wins by knowing its field, not by being strong. Till tomorrow.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 10, Satipatthana Sutta (the four foundations)
